claims.text: Superconductivity in the proposed high-entropy alloy is primarily governed by the combined influence of valence electron concentration and electron-phonon coupling strength.
Changing valence electron concentration modulates the density of states at the Fermi level.
Changes in the density of states at the Fermi level alter electron-phonon coupling strength.
Lattice vibrations mediate electron-phonon coupling in the alloy.
The local bonding environment and lattice structure control the relevant phonon modes.
VEC-induced electronic-structure changes affect the phonon-mediated electron-phonon coupling.
Electron-phonon coupling changes the Cooper-pairing energy gap and thereby changes the superconducting transition temperature under a BCS-like mechanism.
An optimum valence electron concentration should maximize electron-phonon coupling and increase Tc.
Moving the valence electron concentration away from its optimum should reduce Tc.
Incremental compositional substitution with higher- or lower-valence elements can systematically vary the alloy's overall VEC while preserving a homogeneous solid solution.
Relative to the starting alloy, systematic VEC modification will produce correlated changes in Tc.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy remains a single-phase, homogeneously mixed solid solution with minimal disorder effects on electron-phonon coupling.
Significant phase separation or excessive chemical inhomogeneity may invalidate the proposed VEC–electron-phonon-coupling relationship.
Controlled thermal treatments can minimize phase segregation and disorder.
Electron-phonon interactions are expected to dominate at low temperatures near the superconducting transition.
Earlier literature supports the qualitative link between VEC and superconductivity through VEC trends and BCS analyses.
A lack of correlated Tc changes after confirmed VEC modification under maintained phase homogeneity would falsify the hypothesis.
